doc.title: Dave Bennett interviewed by Monk Rowe, via Zoom, April 16, 2025

title: Reading audiences and the old jazz/rockabilly divide
summary: They discuss songs everyone knows, awareness of the crowd while improvising, and how swing-era audiences once resisted 1950s material.

story.theme_name: Where jazz stands today: young players, rock, and the audience
story.community_name: Playing for the audience: communicating from the bandstand

blocks.x: Well you had a parameter there you just mentioned, you get to do what you love. And it always strikes me there are certain songs under the big heading of Americana that just about touch everyone. I mean wouldn’t you be shocked if you did a concert and you sang, “Goodness gracious” and nobody yelled “great balls of fire.”

That would be a strange feeling. I mean even with the differences of age that we play for, there are certain things that everybody knows you know. And so I like to keep that as part of the show, because it draws people in. It gives them something to remember, and they can relate to it.

Do you think — you might not be able to answer this because you’re not other jazz musicians, but do you feel that you pay more attention to the audience when you’re improvising than the typical jazz musician who may be playing more for themselves?

That’s a good question. I don’t know if I can compare myself in that mindset to other people because I don’t know what they’re thinking necessarily, but I know that for me personally I can feel the vibe of a crowd very quickly, you know whether they’re with us or not. I mean my own personal taste, I don’t really go for jazz that’s really far out. That’s just me. I mean as far as jazz goes I’m really drawn to swing and you know, Benny Goodman and Pete Fountain are my heroes and obviously a lot of the guys that you’ve talked to, Kenny Davern and all those. So I think I’m very conscious of where the audience is at. I mean you don’t want to alienate anybody you know. It happens to be, I found in my own path that the crowd enjoys the same things that I enjoy, so it just happens to work out that we’re all pretty much on the same playing field. There may be an occasion — I’d say fifteen years ago it was a little harder to play an old rockabilly tune for a jazz audience because there was more of a segregation and they didn’t grow up with that music. You know the swing era folks maybe didn’t — weren’t on board with

the fifties thing. So it was a little harder, there was more ice to cut through then, so I just didn’t do it as much for those crowds frankly. But now everybody seems to just enjoy a good song you know.
